History:
- Presenting complaint: Acute chest tightness for ~3 hours with associated wheeze, non-productive cough, and mild shortness of breath.
- Onset/duration/progression: Symptoms began ~3 hours prior to consultation; preceded by a viral upper respiratory illness last week (sore throat, runny nose) that is improving but cough and wheeze have persisted. Symptoms somewhat worse at night and with exertion (worse on stairs); not short of breath at rest.
- Context/triggers/previous episodes: Known asthma with prior severe exacerbation requiring intubation in adolescence; reports he ran out of both inhalers ~1 week ago while away at university and has not used them since—likely precipitant. Denies current chest pain; describes inability to get a full breath.
- Associated symptoms: Wheeze, cough (non-productive), prior sore throat/runny nose; denies sputum production in current episode. No drug allergies reported.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (history of severe exacerbation requiring intubation at age ~16–17).
- Atopic history: hay fever, dust allergy; childhood eczema; childhood milk-protein allergy.
- Medications: Salbutamol (Ventolin) — dose/route/frequency not documented; Clenil Modulite (inhaled steroid) — dose/route/frequency not documented. Patient states he has run out of both for ~1 week.
- Allergies: No drug allergies reported. Environmental allergies to dust noted.
- Past hospitalizations/procedures: Prior hospital admission and intubation for asthma in adolescence.
- Social: Student (away at university). Smoking status not documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vital signs: Not recorded.
- General/respiratory exam: No objective vitals or auscultation findings recorded. Patient reports audible wheeze and subjective tightness; not short of breath at rest; increased breathlessness on exertion (stairs). Cough is non-productive.
- Other relevant negatives: No throat swelling reported. No chest pain. Alert and oriented. Formal physical exam findings not recorded.

Impression:
- Primary impression: Acute asthma exacerbation, likely precipitated by recent upper respiratory infection and lapse in inhaled steroid and short-acting bronchodilator use.
- Additional plausible diagnoses consistent with the transcript:
  - Viral bronchitis / post-viral reactive airways disease — supports cough and wheeze after recent URTI and could contribute to symptoms.
  - Community-acquired pneumonia — less likely given lack of fever, productive cough or focal findings but included as lower-probability consideration.
- (No conflict noted between transcript and DDx.)

Management Plan:
- Immediate treatment advised/prescribed:
  - Prescribe replacement inhalers: Salbutamol (Ventolin) and Clenil Modulite inhaler — prescription to be sent (physician stated could be available within ~1 hour). Dose/route/frequency not documented in transcript.
  - Prescribe a short course of oral steroid tablets as discussed: "Two tablets in the morning for five days" (medication name and per-tablet dose not documented).
  - Provide/replace a spacer and written instructions on spacer/inhaler technique.
- Safety-netting and urgent advice:
  - Advise to seek medical attention if increasing shortness of breath, chest pain, light-headedness, or if using salbutamol (Ventolin) more frequently than every 3 hours.
  - If symptoms deteriorate at any time, seek urgent care/emergency services.
- Other advice:
  - Rest and avoid exertion until improved; doctor offered time off work (patient can self-certify first seven days).
  - Read medication labels for steroid side effects; contact clinician with concerns.
- DDx-informed recommendations included where supported by transcript: replacement inhalers, spacer, oral steroid course, and recommendation to re-seek care if increased bronchodilator use or worsening symptoms.

Patient Summary:
- Young adult with known asthma developed acute chest tightness, wheeze and non-productive cough over the past 3 hours after a recent cold and after running out of inhalers for ~1 week. Clinician advised immediate replacement inhalers and a 5-day oral steroid course, provided spacer, and safety-netting for worsening symptoms.

Key Takeaways:
- Restart inhaled therapy immediately (Clenil Modulite as maintenance; Ventolin PRN) — prescriptions being sent.
- Take oral steroid tablets as prescribed: two tablets each morning for five days (medication name/dose not documented).
- Seek urgent medical care if breathlessness worsens, chest pain/light-headedness develops, or if using Ventolin more than every 3 hours.

Next Steps:
- Patient to collect prescribed inhalers and spacer (prescription expected to be sent within ~1 hour per clinician).
- Begin oral steroid course immediately as prescribed.
- Rest and monitor symptoms; obtain GP or urgent review if no improvement or any deterioration.
- Consider objective assessment (peak flow, vitals, SpO2) or clinic assessment if symptoms persist or worsen — arrange follow-up per clinician/GP.

Quality checks:
- Missing but clinically expected elements: vital signs (HR, RR, BP, temperature), oxygen saturation, auscultation findings, peak flow measurement, smoking status, name and dose of oral steroid medication, specific doses/routes/frequencies for inhalers, and any imaging or lab results.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx: None noted.
- Transcript quality comment: Mostly intelligible; occasional audio drop-out/cutting in noted during portions of the steroid counseling.
